name: Midface elevation with blepharoplasty

card.summary: A surgical combination in which lower eyelid surgery is paired with lifting the cheek tissue beneath it, aiming for a shorter lower eyelid, fuller cheeks and a smoother eye-to-cheek line.
card.aka: Midface elevation; midface lift with lower blepharoplasty; transblepharoplasty midface lift
card.note: Surgical procedure by a qualified plastic or oculoplastic surgeon; lower eyelid retraction is a recognised complication.

quick.overview:
Midface elevation repositions the soft tissue of the cheeks upward, and surgeons often combine it with lower eyelid surgery (blepharoplasty) so the lid and cheek are treated as one unit. The aim is a shorter-looking lower eyelid, fuller cheek contour and a smoother transition between eye and cheek.

The literature is mostly surgeon-reported case series and technique papers, along with comparative studies from functional repair of lower eyelid retraction. Reviews describe variation in technique and call for objective long-term outcome data for some approaches.
quick.how: Surgeons describe several routes: through the lower eyelid incision, through the mouth or temple, or endoscopically. Tissue under the cheek is released and lifted and held with sutures, devices or bony fixation, and the lateral corner of the eyelid is often supported at the same time. It is usually done under local or general anaesthesia, and recovery involves swelling and bruising.
quick.risks: Reported risks include lower eyelid retraction or ectropion, dry or irritated eyes, asymmetry, scarring, swelling and need for revision. Surgeons often add a canthopexy to support the lower lid to reduce that risk. The procedure should be assessed and performed by a qualified surgeon after consultation.

lead: Midface elevation with blepharoplasty is a facial plastic and oculoplastic approach in which the soft tissues of the cheek are lifted at the same time as the lower eyelid is operated on. Surgeons describe the middle third of the face as one of the harder areas to rejuvenate, and no single technique has become dominant. [1][2]

The appearance goal is a lower lid that looks shorter, a fuller and higher cheek, and a smoother lid-cheek junction. One 2001 paper describing a combined approach summarised youthful features as eyes that are narrow, short lower lids and full cheeks, and presented the combination as restoring those attributes while avoiding some after-effects of other facial surgery. [3]

The same lifting techniques are also used functionally to correct lower eyelid retraction, for example after surgery or in facial nerve palsy. [4][5] Studies of these cases supply much of the measurable outcome data.

chain: Cheek soft tissue lifted and fixed higher
Support for the lower eyelid and outer corner
Shorter lower lid and fuller cheek
angle.text: The lift moves cheek tissue upward while the lower eyelid is treated, so the lid and cheek change together. It is used for aesthetic rejuvenation and to correct lower-lid retraction or drooping.

paras: Lower blepharoplasty addresses fat protrusion, skin laxity and the eyelid-cheek contour, and can be done through an incision under the lashes or on the inner surface of the lid. Wikipedia notes that adjunctive techniques may include midface elevation or fat repositioning to smooth the transition between lower lid and cheek. [6]

Midface elevation aims at the cheek tissue that has descended or lacks projection. Reviews describe a trend towards less manipulation of midface soft tissue, hidden incisions and endoscopic or percutaneous techniques that allow rejuvenation in younger patients. [7]

Published techniques include endoscopic lifts performed through the brow or temple, [2][8] subperiosteal lifts anchored with drill holes at the inferior orbital rim, [9] lifts with fixation devices, [9] and approaches done through a lower-lid incision, called transblepharoplasty. [10] A comparative study of 27 patients found a drill-hole subperiosteal lift performed similarly to preperiosteal suture fixation and a device-based lift, with no significant complications over a follow-up of more than four months. [9]

Lateral canthal support is a frequent companion. Anatomical work on the lateral canthal tendon notes that eyelid support is advised when midface elevation through a lower-lid approach or conventional blepharoplasty is performed in patients with laxity. [11]

Thread and barbed-suture suspension has been proposed as a less invasive alternative. A review of six studies found mostly minor, short-lived adverse events but unclear peak correction and longevity, with no systematic objective long-term follow-up. [1]

Published work consists largely of surgeon-reported series and retrospective comparisons. A retrospective study of 20 patients per group compared a lateral canthal resuspension with and without midface lift against a lateral tarsal strip, measuring eyelid aperture and canthal height on photographs. [12] A randomized study of 26 patients with lower eyelid retraction compared dermis and auricular cartilage grafts and reported a significant improvement in lid margin position in both groups. [4] Series in facial nerve palsy report midface elevation as part of treating lower-lid malposition and ocular exposure. [5][13]

Eyelid retraction, which can cause dry-eye symptoms and corneal problems, is a recognised consequence of cosmetic surgery and trauma, and its mechanism is described as involving canthal tendon laxity, scarring of the middle lamella and descent of the cheek. [14] Surgeons who describe transblepharoplasty midface work emphasise avoiding complications through lessons learned from treating them. [15]
Barbed-suture lifts have reported mostly minor adverse events; for flap-based lifts, the literature describes issues such as asymmetry, scarring and the need for revision. [1][7]

The procedure sits in the hardmaxx category of surgical changes aimed at midface support, cheek projection and eye area. In these discussions it is treated as an option for people with a long lower lid or flat cheek, with the surgeon's choice of technique being the topic of debate.

timeline.event: Karl Ferdinand von Gräfe coins the term blepharoplasty for eyelid repair. [6]
A combined subperiosteal midface and blepharoplasty approach is reported in a 28-patient series. [3]
Reviews describe a shift toward less invasive, endoscopic and percutaneous midface lifts. [7]
Barbed polypropylene sutures are described for midface elevation. [16]
